text:
Borrow Hindsight
I sometimes ask: “How would I respond to this once I understood it more clearly, in balance and with compassion?” It’s a question borrowed from your future self, and I wouldn’t take their answer as gospel. I don’t think a perfect Higher Self is waiting in there with the answers, either (more on that in How This Relates to IFS).
That future you also knows why you can’t pull this off perfectly today. What would they do for you, if they were here? Maybe they’d just make you some food. (A “no” or a pause can count as the food, too.) If you can’t picture them, make the food yourself, and don’t bother faking a feeling first.
You can borrow a wiser future version of whoever else is involved, too, as long as you don’t assume they’ll end up on your side, or sorry. What the current one keeps doing is still what you go by, however good the picture looks (the future one has never called you back).

Remember When You Already Did It
My father often suggested folks remember a similar-level (or even harder) challenge that they were able to handle. Maybe you survived a car crash and surgery a few years ago, but now you’re having trouble with emotional eating. You can draw strength from the past. As my sister, a historian, likes to say, “The past didn’t go anywhere.” Your own challenge can be less dramatic than a car crash, as long as it really happened. So who or what helped you get through it? Is one piece of that still within reach? If you catch yourself thinking “I survived a car crash, so why can’t I stop eating when I’m upset?”, that’s the past turned into a stick to hit yourself with. Maybe you’re more worn out now, or missing whatever helped back then. (If no example comes to mind, try another doorway.)

So inner child therapy draws on those higher vantage points more concretely. The inner Guide is the closest thing here to a Higher Self, and it has to work with the Nurturer and Protector and come after them. It can’t act like some transcendent authority that waves everything away. Most reparenting doesn’t do enough with the Guide, and IFS goes to the opposite extreme, so I’m trying to bring together the best of both. IFS isn’t exactly one system, so I may be simplifying it here. It has its own branches and disputes, and that’s one more problem I’m trying to remedy by laying all this out systematically in this guide.
IFS calls these wounded young parts “exiles.” I find that pathologizing. I prefer to speak of a child who needs parenting and integration, rather than naming them by their wounded or excluded condition.
And the parts just keep coming: managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts... At some point it’s a maze, with a little one somewhere in the middle of it. Some practitioners are gentle about it and walk you through the maze just fine. Others seem to leave people more split up than when they started. A big institute and a pile of certificates won’t tell you whether a model is true, or whether it’s safe for you.

Borrow One Competency at a Time
A complete ideal parent may be impossible to imagine (unless you saw The Brady Bunch). And imagination is pretty hard for adults anyway since it kinda gets stamped out of kids at an early age, but it’s not just a foolish waste of time. It’s actually a genius mode unlock. So since the adult is actually a baby when it comes to power to imagine, start small: Borrow one function at a time from a figure who embodies it. Perhaps a therapist or your grandmother really cared for you. Perhaps your teacher at some age was a great guide. Maybe an older sibling protected you well. And there’s always your future healed self if you can imagine that.
For warmth, think of someone you remember fondly. How would they sit beside your little one? Just make sure it’s someone who liked you the way you were.
For protecting, ask what a minimally competent adult would do here. Maybe something simple, like actually smelling that old food you’re about to eat and then trashing it if it smells a little weird, or hitting pause before you send an angry text. If the room itself triggers your spidey sense, leave, or lock the door and get help. Even if this still feels like the child acting like the adult, for now, that’s ok. “Fake it til you make it” isn’t exactly it, but yeah. Afterward, you can tell your little one, “I did that for us. That was the Protector.” If it sounds funny, laugh!
The Guide can be you too, just a calmer you. That’s a lot easier to imagine than your future healed self. Think back to what (and how) you decided about something like this the last time you were calm. Or ask what the wise person you respect would have you practice today. A wise tradition (like “What would Jesus do?” or “What would Buddha do?”) can give some direction, too, until you develop your own internal compass.

Part of building who you are is untangling yourself from whatever pulls you away from your own knowing in return for belonging. A political tribe might expect consistent positions and predictable reactions. A family or religion that’s kind to you might have expectations too, but they just feel like being good. Most groups expect some conformity, and that much is ordinary. Your family might want a particular kind of son or daughter, and your friends might have rules about what you can joke about or get upset about. But if going along means betraying yourself, that’s the bargain. It can help to write down the rules your family ran on, including unspoken ones like “Boys don’t cry.” Then write down the role you got handed, like the stand-in parent, or the one who got blamed for everything (ST-CA has lists of both, in sections 15.2.3 and 15.2.4).

Maybe you feel vulnerable, or there’s a tightness in your throat. Maybe you’re sad or scared, or it’s more like you’re trying to protect something. If so, call upon your Nurturer. If you don’t feel better, or if it continues being hostile towards you, stop trying to deal with it and return to your body and the room.
Finding out whether it’s a guard can wait, and you may not be able to comfort it quickly. Is this way of responding helping you be clearer and steadier? Less hooked?

In one of the Buddha’s own accounts of how he woke up, ill will shows up in his mind and he sees it’s hurting him. If he had to figure that out by watching, it’s not obvious. Ill will can make you feel powerful. Being on fire would too, and people would definitely get out of your way, but unless you’re the Human Torch from the Fantastic Four, you’d be the one burning. Has ill will ever left anybody at ease, with nothing to regret afterward?

Where it really differs is spirituality. Schema therapy doesn’t build it in, which isn’t so surprising, since it grew out of cognitive therapy. Still, the preface to its main textbook calls blending it with meditation or religious practice an important development, and some people do blend them. Tara Bennett-Goleman’s book Emotional Alchemy, for one, fits a Buddhist loving-kindness wish to each schema. Her book barely mentions gratitude, and for me that’s the door to the bigger love back in Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED! IFS goes overboard the other way, in my opinion (more on that in the next section).

Say you keep coming back from trip after trip confused or spaced out. That’s the milder stuff, but I’d count it too. If it gets bad, or it keeps happening when you’re sober, I wouldn’t wait to see a psychiatrist about it. And if you think a medicine you’re on is part of the problem, ask your doctor before you stop. Benzos, for one, can be dangerous to quit all at once, and so can alcohol once your body depends on it.

Inner child love
Put your hand over your heart and your other hand on your solar plexus (the two-hand practice in Working with your inner child), and say to yourself in a loving way, “Little one, you are not alone. You don’t have to fix this problem. I’m here now to listen to you.” Make sure you're actually talking to your inner child, even if the words come from a script. If you can't find any warmth today, there's no need to fake it. Just rest your hands there and notice what you find.
Anxiety script
A script you could use for anxiety is:
Where are my body parts? What are my feet doing? How is my body positioned in the chair? How is my body breathing? How is my body situated in the room?
If you’re there, little one, I’m here. Thank you, guard, for letting me know you’re here. You didn’t have to scream. I got your message.
If there is something we need to do, let me know what the first thing is that we need to do at this moment. If there is nothing to do, help my body stand down. I’m not going to abandon you, but I’m not going to worship you either. I will listen to what you have to say and reality test it and then take some action.

The closest thing I can compare it to is the out-of-body part of some near-death experiences. People sometimes report seeing things from impossible angles, and some of those reports (controversially) were verified by others in the room. My room event had nothing like that to check, though, since I wasn’t floating around noticing any details. So those cases can’t back mine up, but they do help me show what I mean by an experience that wasn’t stuck at the body’s vantage point anymore. If you want to go down that rabbit hole, there’s this systematic analysis of near-death reports and the AWARE-II cardiac-arrest study. There’s also a recent veridical-NDE evidence scale.

When you start approaching your inner child, one important thing to become aware of is your inherited parent script. It’s a collection of rules and ways of treating yourself that you adopted as a child, mostly based on how your parent(s) treated you. It doesn’t always take the form of a voice. And don’t confuse it with the inner adult (Nurturer, Protector, Guide) that you consciously build. Often this script acts as a critic or warden, telling your inner child not to cry, not to be “needy”, not to embarrass them, not to be too independent, etc. So when you begin talking to your child in a new, loving way, the script may jump in to say that what you’re doing is “fake”.

Pattern 10: Meta Model questions — the de-hypnosis tool
To 'Milton Model' is to open things up, so the listener can fill in what fits for them. To 'Meta Model' is to stop and ask, "What do you mean by that?" In order to be ethical with people, you need to do both.
When something sounds true but vague, ask, "What do you mean, specifically?" Then, "According to who? Compared to what?" If you hear "always" or "never," check whether it's really every time. If someone's afraid of doing something, ask what exactly would happen if they did. And ask how they know, and what evidence would change their mind.
So when someone is starting to tense up in their body, use the Milton Model to help them soften, and reach for the Meta Model when you feel you're losing track of what's really going on.

Sometimes you have a really good session where you feel how much you care about your little one and say what they needed to hear, and then a few days later you’re skipping lunch and saying yes to everything again. For a lot of people the first thought is that they didn’t go deep enough. I doubt that’s the problem, and the session doesn’t sound like a failure to me. Try a tiny bit of what you did for your little one as you go about your day, because one small thing like that can teach them more than ten more good meditations. You could text a friend that you’re having a rough day instead of saying you’re fine, for instance, and sending that text can be harder than the meditation was.

In SN 22.22 the Buddha puts the weight in one place and the carrying in another. The five aggregates are the burden, and craving is what picks it up. The tangle is heavy all by itself (even an arahant still feels the first dart), and craving is why we keep lugging it around. Physics backs this up, and I mean literally: quarks supply less than 1% of a proton’s mass, and roughly 99% comes from gluon-binding energy. Matter weighs what its binding weighs, and light weighs nothing.

After the day, look at what actually happened. If you did the Protector action(s), not feeling better right away is information to learn from. It doesn’t mean failure. Healing doesn’t go in a straight line, and sometimes standing up for yourself might make you feel worse at first. Not doing it is harder to figure out. Fear is the first guess, but maybe you didn’t know how or why. Being worn out can stop you too, and sometimes whoever said they’d help couldn’t make it. Hey, we’ve all been there. 🤗

The closest comparison that’s worth mentioning is the out-of-body perception in some near-death experiences. People sometimes report seeing things from impossible angles, and a controversial subset of those reports were verified by others in the room. Those cases had a target that other people could check. My room experience didn’t, since I wasn’t floating around noticing specific details, so those cases can’t vouch for it. They still help show what I mean by an experience that wasn’t stuck at the body’s vantage point anymore. If you want to dig in, there’s this systematic analysis of near-death reports, the AWARE-II cardiac-arrest study, and a recent veridical-NDE evidence scale.

Scientists can only circle the edges of consciousness, though they find some wild stuff out there: people functioning with no felt controller, and several things cognized at once. Split-brain patients can seem like two knowers sharing a skull, and one recent theory models minds as nested parallel observers. The full nerdy tour is in the research report. Science gives my argument a third wheel, making it safer to ride, but it will never show nibbāna itself – self and sense organs unweaving into self-presenting light flows of bliss. That requires meditation.

With that under you, you can get a lot less desperate about belonging with people. Not all at once, but the Guide keeps watching for the moment your little one starts thinking, “If they stop liking me, I won’t belong anywhere,” and keeps reminding it that a group’s approval isn’t the deepest belonging there is. By the way, this job doesn’t have to be called the Guide. The Wise One works, or your Inner Teacher, and “Guru” does for some people.

I think most people who chase spiritual freedom are also trying to get away from something painful in themselves, and a lot of it goes back to childhood. That’s spiritual bypassing. Plenty of seekers and gurus do it (I’ve written about the Dalai Lama as one example), and I did it too. It doesn’t mean you’re stupid or crazy.

I used to attribute “life is like a dream” directly to the historical Buddha, until I found out the famous stanza I loved is from the later Mahāyāna Diamond Sutra, which puts some words in his mouth. The early Pāli texts already had the same kind of pictures, though. In SN 22.95 form is like foam, feeling is like a bubble, perception is a mirage and consciousness is a magic trick, and Dhammapada 170 tells us to look at the world like a bubble, or a mirage.

If you feel vulnerable, a tightness in your throat, sadness or fear, or like you’re trying to protect something, call upon your Nurturer. If you don’t feel better, or it keeps being hostile towards you, stop trying to deal with it and return to your body and the room.
Finding out whether it’s a guard can wait, and you may not be able to comfort it quickly. Is this way of responding helping you to be clearer and steadier and less hooked?

Remember When You Already Did It

Maybe you survived a car crash and surgery a few years ago, but now you’re having trouble with emotional eating. You can draw strength from the past. So who or what helped you get through it? Is one piece of that still within reach? If you catch yourself thinking “I survived a car crash, so why can’t I stop eating when I’m upset?”, that’s the past turned into a stick to hit yourself with. Maybe you’re more worn out now, or missing whatever helped back then. (If no example comes to mind, try another doorway.)

For many people, healing does get around to some forgiveness eventually, or at least to not being run by the resentment anymore. It can’t be put on a schedule. And no, you don’t have to forgive first to get safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice or get better. Then again, when you’re actively resentful you get tunnel vision, and your little one’s world keeps revolving around the injury. And if someone pressures you into forgiving early, you end up with an enlightened-looking act, while the wound goes underground.

Forgiveness without bypass
We cannot force forgiveness on ourselves. It has to come from a place of understanding, otherwise it can be bypassing. But if we stay in the anger forever, we let the injury dictate how we live our lives in the present. Holding all of this just means remembering that it can all be true at once. They really did hurt us and they still have to answer for it. We have to keep our boundary with them, especially after forgiveness, which can weaken it. One day we may find that we have forgiven them for not knowing better, just like Jesus did on the Cross.
You might say to the part of you that got hurt, “I’m not going to use spiritual mumbo jumbo to shush your cries and make you forgive before you're ready. But I’m also not going to build our whole life around this wound forever.”
Forgiving yourself
For self-forgiveness, name what you regret doing, and take responsibility for just that part. Let yourself feel the remorse by taking in the harm done, and see how it went against your values. Just stop short of making yourself a permanent criminal by identifying with the behaviors you're now abandoning.
Do what you can to put it right. Every so often, come back to how you got to be someone who could do that, until you understand the pattern well enough that it can't drive you anymore.

Maybe you’ve let a small child win at Go Fish and never found a good time to start playing for real. Who wants to be the grown-up who finally wins? Without the Guide, you can slide from looking after your little one into spoiling them the same way. Sweets and screens can pass for loving yourself, and so can getting them out of anything hard. Treats and pampering do better at set times, where they can’t get out of hand. They shouldn’t get canceled as a punishment after a bad day, either (ST-CA, section 17.1.4).

Sometimes the session itself goes really well. You feel real care for your little one and say exactly what they needed to hear. And a few days later you’re skipping lunch and saying yes to everything again. A lot of people’s first guess is that they didn’t go deep enough. I don’t think that’s it, though, or that this one failed. Maybe the grown-up just hasn’t come out of the exercise with you yet. Whatever you did for your little one in there, I’d try a tiny bit of it out here, like texting a friend that you’re having a rough day instead of saying you’re fine. That can honestly be harder than the meditation was. One small thing like that can teach your little one more than ten more good meditations.

Sometimes a session goes great, and a few days later you’re skipping lunch and saying yes to everything again. Going deeper next time won’t fix that, because you just haven’t brought any of it out with you yet. Whatever you did for your little one in there, try a tiny bit of it out here, like texting a friend that you’re having a rough day instead of saying you’re fine.

Say you keep feeling confused or spaced out afterward. That’s one of the milder reactions, but those count as caution signs too. If any of this is severe or risky, get professional help right away, especially if it keeps going or comes back while you’re sober. And if a prescribed medicine, or anything your body is dependent on, might be part of the problem, don’t suddenly quit it; have a doctor help you stop safely.

If you’ve had a spiritual opening long before there was much of a Nurturer or Protector around, it can still be real. What I’d look at afterward is what it did to your love. Has that love reached your little one yet? And does anybody notice a difference, like you keeping your word more, or being more patient when someone’s having a hard day?

In SN 22.22 the five aggregates are the burden and craving is what picks it up, so the Buddha splits the accounting between them. The tangle’s heavy by nature (even an arahant feels the first dart), and craving’s what keeps us carrying it. And binding is literally heavy in physics too (quarks supply less than 1% of a proton’s mass, roughly 99% comes from gluon-binding energy). Matter weighs what its binding weighs, and light weighs nothing.

If you ever want to retire the shortcut, stop practicing it, and take it out of your recordings and any apps that play it. Then go back to your usual induction. Decide to retire it while you’re wide awake, and tell yourself so. It might still work on you for a while, though, since saying it’s gone doesn’t erase it overnight. You can also keep it, but only to start a session you’ve chosen ahead of time. If it keeps pulling you in when you don’t want it to, or you come out of it disoriented, find someone qualified to help you with it, like a therapist who knows hypnosis.

Your little one can get really loud in the gap after one life ends and before the next one has formed (Tibetan Buddhism calls an in-between state like that a bardo). A breakup will do it, or moving to another country, an illness, losing your faith or a role, your youngest moving out. Maybe you’ve left a family or community, maybe you’ve stayed on new terms. A therapist or helper might step back because you’re doing so much better, and suddenly your little one is wailing.

A good routine still feels like punishment to your little one if you keep it in the warden’s tone. If talking back to that voice feels disloyal, give it a name of its own, like the Critic. Write its lines down, with who said them and when. Comfort your little one first, then write a reply to each line, firm or funny but never mean (ST-CA has this as an exercise, section 18.12.2).

Your little one can get really loud in the gap after one life ends and before the next one has formed. A breakup will do it, or moving to another country, an illness, losing your faith or a role, your youngest moving out. Maybe you’ve left a family or community, maybe you’ve stayed on new terms. A therapist or helper might step back because you’re doing so much better, and suddenly your little one is wailing. For a while the old you is gone and the new you hasn’t shown up yet, the kind of in-between state Tibetan Buddhism calls a bardo.

As for telling whether it helped, a few hours of feeling lighter, with the old feeling back the same day, is a few hours of relief. I’d take that! I just wouldn’t say the problem’s solved based on that, or give the exercise all the credit, especially if you also slept well for once. Jot down what changed and how long it lasted if you want, and then leave it alone.
How many tries is enough? I really don’t know, and I’d be suspicious of anyone who promises you a number, including you, since some things shift in a day and some take about as long as learning guitar. If it’s making things worse, or you just can’t do it right now, I’d change course sooner (stopping counts). Not wanting to do it anymore is a reason too, but if that “nope” sounds like a part of you that’s trying to protect you, I’d hear it out first. If it still says no, that’s your answer. And if you keep following the reparenting steps correctly without getting the expected results, consider if you have a unique case these steps don’t match yet. Maybe you’ll find something that works better for you, or you can ask me what I’d do for this case, or ask a therapist you work with. Either way, I’d like to hear about it!
Sometimes a session goes great, and a few days later you’re skipping lunch and saying yes to everything again. Going deeper next time won’t fix that. You just haven’t brought any of it out with you yet. Whatever you did for your little one in there, try a tiny bit of it out here, like texting a friend that you’re having a rough day instead of saying you’re fine.

Differentiation is slow, and it goes on your whole life. If a family, group or relationship won’t let you do this while you’re still part of it, temporary distance may be necessary. And sometimes you need the break anyway, because it’s hard to hear what you actually want while the old programming is still playing in your ear. Some people come back later on different terms. Sometimes the leaving turns out to be permanent, because going back would mean disappearing again. You don’t have to know yet which one yours is, since you learn to tell the difference as you differentiate.

Or if you do get an answer, it could come in different forms, like a voice or just a hunch, though it’s often more like a feeling. Maybe grief or anger. Then just listen and be present for it, if that’s what it wants. If it tells you to do something, I’d only do it if it’s loving and leaves you free, and it should make sense too. Even then, anything big or hard to undo can wait until you’re calm and you’ve checked it against what you actually know.

I dream of a way to work in depth that isn’t run by a guru, and a way of being in a community with distributed authority. A place where people who’ve done the healing first can join, and don’t have to pretend they’re fully finished. It would also have peer practice and enough play that it doesn’t become a permanent repair shop.

If the Love Isn’t Coming Yet
If you weren’t loved well as a child, “love your inner child” can sound like nonsense. Love them how? Maybe you really want the best for your little one. Maybe you hug them in your imagination, or miss them. And you can still feel none of the warmth people mean when they say love. That doesn’t close the door, though, it just means you start smaller.
Maybe just imagining a caring grown-up makes you feel more threatened, or lonelier. Lonelier is a strange one, with somebody right there. Then go smaller still, to the least cruel response a decent adult could offer your little one. It’s scaffolding, and it isn’t a test of whether you were loved enough.
Once you take the hostility out, there’s room for warmth. What people most often say helped is letting their defenses down. I mean by choice, after the part guarding you has been heard. If you’ve never been safe being loved, your ego can act like a rigid security guard that won’t let the feeling in, and being vulnerable is the opening the feeling needs. (This guard is only about letting the feeling in. People still have to earn your trust.) Sometimes the warmth is there, with a cold part standing in front of it, guarding something. That part tends to step aside once it’s been heard (see the section Hear the Guard First).
If the love still isn’t coming, you can at least stop judging your little one. Obviously no insults. Helpful advice is great, we all need advice. Let them absorb it at their pace. And don’t expect a thank-you for the session, like they booked it. That’s enough to start being the adult, even if it isn’t enough yet for them to trust you. Trust takes warmth, and if there isn’t any yet, borrow some.
Your little one might not take it well at first. 😜 More like “Oh, so NOW you care?” Your first instinct might be “But I’m trying!” Some days, just hearing it out like a decent adult is the only thing you’ll manage to borrow.

I think the opposite trap can feel a lot like finally having your act together. It’s forced adulthood, and it sounds like “Nope, all good!” from somebody with a fever who’s cleaning the whole kitchen anyway. Not a lot of fun in that kitchen, and nobody gets very close to the person in it. If that’s you, clamping down harder is going to feel like the fix, but it’s just more of the same. I’d try croaking to someone you trust, “Could you pick up some soup?” If you keep swinging between spoiling and clamping down, try staying warm while you say what happens next, like “Not now, we’ll go after lunch.”
Once a need does show, after all that hiding, it’s okay to want a lot of closeness. So then someone you love goes for a walk alone, and you’ve texted “hello??” before they’re at the corner. When they get back, you sulk all night. Wanting them close is fine! Blowing up their phone and sulking all night is a different story. Your Guide could help you ask for what you need instead, like a hug before they go and a rough idea of when they’ll be back. Before any of that, though, I’d let your little one say what’s going on. I think it just wants to know they’re coming back.
The Guide doesn’t need to know everything for sure (that would be an OCD Guide, and then you’d need a Guide for the OCD Guide). It chooses the next sane step that fits your values based on the info available, and that’s how it helps your little one grow toward a whole life. Waiting to be sure first is sometimes proper & prudent, but if it’s a pattern, it can keep life on hold, and then your little one’s world stays small. Sometimes something really is stuck on someone else’s end (you’ve asked, and followed up, and there’s nothing left for you to do yet), and waiting on that isn’t avoidance. The Guide can let it wait, keeping an eye out for when it frees up, and keep the rest of your life moving.

When the Practice Feels Real but Stays Shallow
Some people have the opposite problem. It feels like you’re connecting with your little one, but the contact is staying near the surface. Meditating for a long time and then sleeping can open up much more emotionally direct stuff, especially in a second sleep, after you’ve already slept once. I could tell the daytime pl/ork had stayed shallow from the difference at night. If you wake up from a dream soaked in way more feeling and need than anything the session got near, this is probably you. A nice session that just wears off is a different thing. I’d ask what the dream let you feel that the session didn’t, and look at it again after your morning coffee. And if nightmares start wrecking your sleep, dial the practice down by doing it earlier in the day, or for less time.

Not Every Hero Wears A Cape
Set one boundary. “What’s a ‘boundary’?”, I might be asking. That looks like saying no to something that’s costing you too much (money, time, whatever it is). Handle that task you’ve been putting off, or the tax man, or your DUIs in Maryland, even if all you do today is open the envelope. Keep one small promise to your little one. Clean your room! Maybe your little one had grown-ups who said sweet things and then did nothing, and maybe you’ve done it too, so this is how they start to believe you.
You can protect your little one from yourself too, like by repairing after an internal attack. “What’s an ‘internal attack’?” Calling yourself an idiot for losing your keys again, for one. Your little one was listening, so you go back and apologize to them, and if they’re sarcastic about it, you hear it out instead of snapping back (they don’t trust you yet, and you don’t ask them to). If they complain about something and they’re right, you say so. All of that shows them, as clearly as the clean room did, that you’re safe to be around and that you accept them. Love needs both, but without warmth they can still feel like they’re only being put up with.
Plenty of people are still at the putting-up-with part. Even with little or no warmth for your little one yet, the relationship can start with the Protector’s plain acts, and the warmth can come after. That feels backwards, since you’d think you have to feel it first before you could do anything for them. But yeah, bonding starts somewhere. And this is not to say you’ve never done anything to care for yourself. If not, you’d be dead right now. But now we’re doing more of it on purpose, as a base for love to grow.

Some families run on a bargain like “If I’m happy while someone I love is suffering, I’m abandoning them.”
That’s exactly why I was crying for 14 years. Beginning at the age of 12, when I really started to understand that life is brutal for most people, I became convinced that being happy myself, while others weren’t, was selfish. I had this poster in my room that really resonated with me, by the famous socialist, Eugene V. Debs. I told this to a therapist in college and she actually agreed it was a good reason to be depressed!
Once I started cultivating my own happiness, I found I got a lot better at helping other people toward theirs. That might not be how it goes for everyone. And no, it doesn’t mean unhappy people can’t help. Do your part for people who are suffering, and skip the part where you have to be miserable too.
Some friends or family really might not like it when you get happier, though. Someone might pull away, or keep dragging you back into the old misery. I’d take that loss seriously, and look at what they do and what you owe them, before deciding it’s envy.
I’d still try a small good thing, like a nice meal, and see what actually happens.

When you’re approaching your inner child, it’s important to be aware of the parent script you inherited. It’s made up of the rules and ways of treating yourself that you picked up as a child, mostly from how your parent(s) treated you. It doesn’t always come as a voice, and it isn’t the inner adult (Nurturer, Protector, Guide) that you consciously build. Often this script acts as a critic or warden, telling your inner child not to cry, not to be “needy”, not to embarrass them, not to be too independent, etc. So when you begin talking to your child in a new, loving way, the script may jump in to say that what you’re doing is “fake”.

The Parent You Inherited
I’d look at the parent “script” you inherited: how you learned to treat yourself from how people treated you growing up, long before you started building your Nurturer, Protector and Guide. It can be warm, but it’s often more like a critic, or a warden with rules. The rules can even sound reasonable, like “You can come back to the table when you’re done with your embarrassing crying fit.” If yours was like that, your little one learned bit by bit to hide whatever part of their real self wasn’t allowed, so they could keep belonging. They might still be doing it.
If it’s a critic, the parent you inherited also measures whatever you show the world against an impossible ideal, and then attacks you from both sides: you’re not good enough, and anything that does look good is fake anyway. That second one means nothing you do could ever count, and it’s one place feeling fake can come from. When a new grown-up voice shows up saying “Trust me,” of course your little one doesn’t answer.
But with the borrowed adulthood trick, the new grown-up can start outside your head, as someone who likes you the way you are, or as something you do to protect your little one, like letting the phone ring when you know how that call goes. You don’t have to pretend to feel anything to let a phone ring. Your little one can watch you do it many times before trusting you, while the parent you inherited calls it fake.
A good routine still feels like lockdown to your little one when it’s run in the warden’s tone. Talking back to the warden can feel disloyal, so I’d give that voice a name of its own, like the Critic. Then start a little rap sheet of its lines, with who used to say them and when (ST-CA has this as an exercise, section 18.12.2). Comfort your little one before you answer any of it. Your answers can be firm or funny, as long as they aren’t mean, since mean is the Critic’s department.
The voice can also pile on. You feel sad, then call yourself pathetic for being sad, and now you’re ashamed and want to hide. You could probably have handled the sadness on its own. The name-calling, though, is where your Nurturer can step in.

That part doesn’t have to move out. It’s been living there way longer than the grown-up you, and it can keep watch while you take one small step toward your little one. I think watching is what it wants anyway, to find out if there’s a grown-up here now who could call it all off if things got to be too much. It doesn’t have to be all or nothing, either. Maybe for now it would settle for a lighter cover, like blinds tilted open a crack, and let you peek out for a minute (ST-CA, section 9.3.4). If it says no, I’d listen. When it lets you, keep an eye on that part too, for any change at all.

The 15-minute daily practice
You don't need to learn a second script for this. It's the same process (gather your attention, notice what's here, respond, wait, and come all the way back), just for fifteen minutes or so. That is long enough to induce yourself (it only takes a few minutes), practice and let it unfold at its own pace, and come out again (that takes a few minutes too). Fifteen minutes is just a handy appointment with yourself, though, and your feelings don't have to keep to it. Five minutes is plenty to see what happens when you simply sit in silence, listening, and you can interrupt yourself at any time to change direction if that feels better.
You can also try other ways of inducing yourself, such as becoming aware of 3 things you can see, 3 things you can hear, 3 things you can feel in your body; then 2 of each, 1 of each. Then count from 5 to 1 and begin to listen. Choose one way to induce yourself. You don't need to try all of them (in fact, stacking them might be counter-productive).
Once you have practiced listening a few times with the recordings, you may want to shorten them to speed up your induction, or even practice without playing them back at all. On the other hand, if you like using the recordings, there is no reason to stop. (Once you know the induction well, the cue from "A shortcut back into hypnosis" can shorten it too.)
As you come out of the process, ask yourself what needed warmth, and what needed to be protected. What do you need to do differently to be more in accord with truth and love and life? Is there something you want to explore more fully or a capacity you want to build? And most importantly, what can you now carry yourself that you used to have to borrow? If you identified something you needed to do differently, make a plan with yourself to do that thing. The more specific you can be, the more likely you are to change: “If _________ (fill in the cue for the old pattern), then I will do ________ (fill in a small action that will begin to change the pattern).” Then check back later and see how you are doing – sleeping, relating, functioning, etc., not only how impressive the session felt.

I used to attribute “life is like a dream” directly to the historical Buddha, but the famous stanza I loved turns out to be from the later Mahāyāna Diamond Sutra, which puts some words in his mouth. The early Pāli texts were already reaching for the same kind of pictures, though. In SN 22.95 form is like foam, feeling is like a bubble, perception is a mirage and consciousness is a magic trick, and Dhammapada 170 tells us to look at the world like a bubble, or a mirage.

To turn this off, stop rehearsing it, take it out of any recordings you have and any apps that are active, and go back to the regular induction you’ve been using. Say that you won’t use it anymore when you’re awake, but just saying it’s gone won’t make it go away immediately. If you find you’re responding to it when you don’t want to, or you’re getting disoriented after using it, get some help from someone qualified. You can keep it in if you want, but only as a way to start a session later, when you want to. For now, today’s trance will be over when you come out of it.
When you come out of it, reverse anything you’ve done to alter your state. If you’ve floated, regain your weight (of your choice, of course), and if you’ve shrunk, grow back to your normal size. If you’ve regressed or met parts, come back to feeling complete in the here and now, and acknowledge that your body belongs to you and is under the control of the adult mind. If you’ve gone somewhere, go back the same way. Etcetera. Make sure the only things you bring out with you are the ones you want to.

Aside from focusing on things in your direct experience, you can also suggest yourself into greater alertness (it's still relaxed-alert, not paranoid-alert). Keep your eyes open. Use a small hand movement each time you make the auto-suggestion that you're gaining increasing clarity. Then stop the hand movement and see where your mind is at. That hand movement is the mental escape into the body's flow. Say something like,
“Starting with your eyes open, press your thumb to your forefinger, gently, and let go. Each time you do, you get a little more awake… Press and let go again, a bit clearer. And once more, and now you’re clearer than when you started. Now stop pressing. In the first second after you stop, is the pressing still echoing somewhere? Start with your fingers, which may still be tingling. Did your breath keep the rhythm going? Is your attention still waiting for the next press? Or maybe there’s no echo at all. Just notice. Then sit up straight and work from this level.”

Sometimes care isn’t the main thing missing. A meal can help, and so can a boundary, but does that actually get at the deeper existential question underneath? Life shouldn’t be just something you endure, like a hamster wheel or a rat race. What would you need to bring zest to a life of discovery?

Differentiation is slow, and it goes on your whole life. If a family, group or relationship won’t let you do this while you’re still part of it, you may need some distance for a while. And sometimes you need the break anyway, because it’s hard to hear what you actually want while the old programming is still playing in your ear. Some people come back later on different terms, and sometimes the leaving turns out to be permanent, because going back would mean disappearing again. There’s no need to know yet which one yours is, since you learn to tell the difference as you differentiate.

The personal accounts and the way I arrange this practice are my own, especially adaptations like combining body-oriented work and hypnotic work. So far, this combination hasn't been scientifically validated as a treatment. The Cochrane Collaboration has not yet awarded me their highest medal of honor.
Learning, entering, and returning
Healing the Divided Self, Maggie Phillips and Claire Frederick (1995), pp 24-27, 45-50, 83-90, covers a lot of aspects of this post, such as interactive hypnosis, helping the subject learn how to learn by using other senses, learning self hypnosis, making sure the subject comes back at the end, etc. However, this is a professional clinical book, not a self help book, so be careful about trying to use the procedures used with the cases, etc in this book for solo work (and the same goes for its historical claims). Also, Adam Eason and Benjamin Parris's article about self hypnosis for the International Society of Hypnosis should be a useful thing to read (especially the parts that talk about how to learn to learn when you're directing it yourself, and about whether you need another person to help you, and using recordings to help you, etc.)
Indirect language and re-entry cues
For information about using indirect hypnotic language patterns, such as pacing, utilizing, metaphor, and associational cues, etc, see Healing the Divided Self, Phillips and Frederick, 1995, pp 53-57, 96-100, as well as Nimja's tutorial on hypnotic language patterns, and his tutorial on triggers. That's where these techniques come from, but don't blame them for every NLP claim here, or for an example that doesn't suit trauma work (Nimja didn't write or endorse this guide). I adapted the language for my own purposes, and I deliberately used a sequence that would be easy to use for re-entry.

A good routine still feels like punishment to your little one if it’s kept in the warden’s tone. If talking back to that voice feels disloyal, give it a name of its own, like the Critic, and write its lines down, with who said them and when. Comfort your little one first, then write a reply to each line, firm or funny but never mean (ST-CA has this as an exercise, section 18.12.2).

Part of building who you are is untangling yourself from whatever pulls you away from your own knowing in return for belonging. A political tribe might expect consistent positions and predictable reactions, and with a family or religion that’s kind to you, the expectations might just feel like being good. Most groups expect some conformity, which is ordinary. Your family might want a particular kind of son or daughter, and your friends might have rules about what you can joke about or get upset about. But if going along means betraying yourself, that’s the bargain. Try writing down the rules your family ran on, unspoken ones included, like “Boys don’t cry,” and then the role you got handed, like the stand-in parent, or the one who got blamed for everything (ST-CA has lists of both, in sections 15.2.3 and 15.2.4).

After the day, look at what actually happened. Say you did the Protector action(s) and you don’t feel any better, or you feel worse. Standing up for yourself can do that at first. Not doing it is harder to figure out. Fear is the first guess, but did you know how to do it, and why? Maybe you were worn out, or whoever said they’d help couldn’t make it. 🤗

Maybe you’ve let a small child win at Go Fish and never found a good time to start playing for real. Who wants to be the grown-up who finally wins? Without the Guide, you can slide from looking after your little one into spoiling them the same way. Sweets and screens can pass for loving yourself, and so can getting them out of anything hard. Treats and pampering do better at set times, where they can’t get out of hand. They shouldn’t get canceled as a punishment after a bad day, either (ST-CA, section 17.1.4).

What’s starving them is anomie. What’s anomie? Well, we evolved to live in small groups where everybody knows everybody, and they love and trust each other. In a large society, the shared norms and close ties that held those groups together fall apart. Nobody knows anybody well enough, or for long enough, to tell who can be trusted. Even your next-door neighbor is often a total stranger. That’s how large societies end up run by psychopaths. (Yes, I’m always going on about this.)

If you ever want to retire the shortcut, stop practicing it, take it out of your recordings and any apps that play it, and go back to your usual induction. Decide that while you’re wide awake, and tell yourself so. It might still work on you for a while, though, since saying it’s gone doesn’t erase it overnight. You can also keep it, but only to start a session you’ve chosen ahead of time. If it keeps pulling you in when you don’t want it to, or you come out of it disoriented, find someone qualified to help you with it, like a therapist who knows hypnosis.

So inner child therapy draws on those higher vantage points more concretely. The inner Guide is the closest thing here to a Higher Self, and it has to work with the Nurturer and Protector and come after them. It can’t act like some transcendent authority that waves everything away. Most reparenting doesn’t do enough with the Guide, which is the opposite extreme from IFS, so I’m trying to bring together the best of both. IFS isn’t exactly one system, so I may be simplifying it here. It has its own branches and disputes, and that’s one more problem I’m trying to remedy by laying all this out systematically in this guide.
IFS calls these wounded young parts “exiles.” I find that pathologizing. I’d rather speak of a child who needs parenting and integration than name them by their wounded or excluded condition.
And the parts just keep coming: managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts... At some point it’s a maze, with a little one somewhere in the middle of it. Some practitioners are gentle about it and walk you through the maze just fine, while others seem to leave people more split up than when they started. A big institute and a pile of certificates won’t tell you whether a model is true, or whether it’s safe for you.

In SN 22.22 the five aggregates are the burden and craving is what picks it up, so the Buddha splits the accounting cleanly. The tangle’s heavy by nature (even an arahant feels the first dart), and craving’s what keeps us carrying it. And binding is literally heavy in physics too (quarks supply less than 1% of a proton’s mass, roughly 99% comes from gluon-binding energy). Matter weighs what its binding weighs, while light weighs nothing.

A spiritual opening can come long before there’s much of a Nurturer or Protector around, and it can still be real. Afterward, I’d look at what it did to your love. Has it reached your little one yet? And does anybody notice a difference, like you keeping your word more, or being more patient when someone’s having a hard day?

The closest comparison that’s worth mentioning is the out-of-body perception in some near-death experiences. People sometimes report seeing things from impossible angles, and a controversial subset of those reports were verified by others in the room. Those cases had a target that other people could check. My room experience didn’t, since I wasn’t floating around noticing specific details, so those reports can’t vouch for it. But they do help show what I mean by an experience that wasn’t stuck at the body’s vantage point anymore. If you want to dig in, there’s this systematic analysis of near-death reports, the AWARE-II cardiac-arrest study, and a recent veridical-NDE evidence scale.

Science only gets to circle the edges of consciousness, though it finds some wild stuff out there: people functioning with no felt controller, several things cognized at once, split-brain patients who can seem like two knowers sharing a skull, and one recent theory that models minds as nested parallel observers. The full nerdy tour is in the research report. Science gives my argument a third wheel, making it safer to ride, but only meditation will ever show you nibbāna itself – self and sense organs unweaving into self-presenting light flows of bliss.

Borrow Hindsight
I sometimes ask: “How would I respond to this once I understood it more clearly, in balance and with compassion?” It’s a question borrowed from your future self, and I wouldn’t take their answer as gospel. I don’t think a perfect Higher Self is waiting in there with the answers, either (more on that in How This Relates to IFS).
That future you also knows why you can’t pull this off perfectly today. What would they do for you, if they were here? Maybe they’d just make you some food. If you can’t picture them, make the food yourself, and don’t bother faking a feeling first. A “no” or a pause can count as the food, too.
You can also borrow a wiser future version of whoever else is involved, as long as you don’t assume they’ll end up on your side, or sorry. What the current one keeps doing is still what you go by, however good the picture looks (the future one has never called you back).

Five Stages of Reparenting
For now, I think of the whole path in five fairly predictable stages. You might be starting at any point here (and it may change even from hour to hour as well):
1. You’re still stuck identifying as the lost inner child, forced frequently into handling situations that require more maturity, even if it looks like you’ve got it all together. At this stage, use your childlike superpowers to come into the “Wow of Now” (have you seen the movie Waking Life?), and make sure there’s enough safety around you to continue with reparenting.
2. Begin to borrow adulthood — remember watching Mr. Rogers or Sesame Street? Those adult role models are what we’re looking for at this stage. This can almost feel like playing house as a kid where you imagined how you’d take care of a baby doll etc.
3. Practice adulting — do at least one part of caring for yourself while support is still there from the previous step.
4. Adult mode itself — after enough practice with reparenting, you become a natural at sending love to little you, protecting them, and directing them.
5. Adult and child in relationship — the adult leads. The child isn’t pushed away, but doesn’t have to run the whole life alone. This can actually feel really weird if you’ve been stuck in forced adulthood for a while. Our goal is to go from weird to silly and playful. Lose self-consciousness while gaining self-awareness, if that makes sense!
Whichever stage you’re at, saying the right thing when you sit down with your little one helps, but you also have to start actually doing some of it in the rest of your life. Your little one starts believing the grown-up you when they catch you lying down because you’re wiped out, instead of pushing through one more chore.
Reparenting isn’t an exercise you finish, after all. Say your boss asks you to stay late again. You tell them no and go home feeling okay about it, and nobody had to cry on a meditation cushion for that to happen.

The 15-minute daily practice
You don't need to learn a second script for this. It's the same process (gather your attention, notice what's here, respond, wait, and come all the way back), just for fifteen minutes or so. That is long enough to induce yourself (it only takes a few minutes), practice and let it unfold at its own pace, and come out again (that takes a few minutes too). Fifteen minutes is just a handy appointment with yourself, though, and your feelings don't have to keep to it. Five minutes is plenty to see what happens when you simply sit in silence, listening, and you can interrupt yourself at any time to change direction if that feels better.
You can also try other ways of inducing yourself, such as becoming aware of 3 things you can see, 3 things you can hear, 3 things you can feel in your body; then 2 of each, 1 of each. Then count from 5 to 1 and begin to listen. Choose one way to induce yourself. You don't need to try all of them (in fact, stacking them might be counterproductive).
Once you have practiced listening a few times with the recordings, you may want to shorten them to speed up your induction, or even practice without playing them back at all. On the other hand, if you like using the recordings, there is no reason to stop. (Once you know the induction well, the cue from "A shortcut back into hypnosis" can shorten it too.)
As you come out of the process, ask yourself what needed warmth, what needed to be protected, what you need to do differently to be more in accord with truth and love and life. Is there something you want to explore more fully or a capacity you want to build? And most importantly, what can you now carry yourself that you used to have to borrow? If you identified something you needed to do differently, make a plan with yourself to do that thing. The more specific you can be, the more likely you are to change: “If _________ (fill in the cue for the old pattern), then I will do ________ (fill in a small action that will begin to change the pattern).” Then check back later and see how you are doing – sleeping, relating, functioning, etc., not only how impressive the session felt.

When the Practice Feels Real but Stays Shallow
Some people have the opposite problem. It feels like you’re connecting with your little one, but the contact is staying near the surface. Meditating for a long time and then sleeping can open up much more emotionally direct stuff, especially in a second sleep, after you’ve already slept once. What showed me that the daytime pl/ork had stayed shallow was the difference at night. Say you wake up from a dream soaked in way more feeling and need than anything the session got near. Then this is probably you. (A nice session that just wears off is a different thing.) I’d ask what the dream let you feel that the session didn’t, and look at it again after your morning coffee. And if nightmares start wrecking your sleep, dial the practice down by doing it earlier in the day, or for less time.

Maybe it just has something to say. It could be your little one, mad that you took so long to come back, or a part of you that’s trying to protect you. Maybe it’s that parent you inherited, or something from earlier today, or a bit of each. I wouldn’t spend long deciding what to call each part, though. Every part of you learns from how the others treat it, your little one included. Say the protective part warns you about something. When you hear it out, it doesn’t have to get any louder.

Blaming yourself can be protective, too. “It’s all my fault” might be your parent’s line, word for word. Then again, if it’s your fault, maybe you can fix it before they leave. I’d stop the cruelty either way, and get curious about what makes it so hard to give up.

If You Want to Kill Yourself
Maybe you’re reading this about to act, or with the means close by. If so, before anything else, get another human being involved, and put some distance between you and the means. A crisis line counts, and the person on the other end can be a total stranger. Do the same if you can’t stop yourself. Also when you’re badly disoriented or intoxicated, or can’t tell whether any of this is you. If you get safe first, the question of whether life is worth living stays open long enough to look at.
Then, before getting all philosophical, make sure there’s a real, live grown-up in the room or on the phone, if that’s possible. And as for the internal psychology of it, when the part that wants to die feels like all of you, go ahead and notice who’s doing the noticing (as we discussed in Noticing Counts), or borrow an adult from the adult lending library in your head :). Any part of you that can help keep your body safe, or would rather wait on a decision you can’t undo, is welcome. And if none of them shows up yet? No problem, the questions can wait.

Forgiveness without bypass
We cannot force forgiveness on ourselves. It has to come from understanding, otherwise it can be bypassing. But if we stay in the anger forever, we let the injury dictate how we live our lives in the present. So how do we hold all of this? We just remember that it can all be true at once. They really did hurt us and they still have to answer for it. Keeping our boundary with them is crucial, especially after forgiveness, since forgiving tends to weaken it. One day we may find that we have forgiven them for not knowing better, just like Jesus did on the Cross.
You might say to the part of you that got hurt, “I’m not going to use spiritual mumbo jumbo to shush your cries and make you forgive before you're ready. But I’m also not going to build our whole life around this wound forever.”
Forgiving yourself
For self-forgiveness, name what you regret doing, and take responsibility for just that part. Let yourself feel the remorse by taking in the harm done, and see how it went against your values. But stop short of making yourself a permanent criminal by identifying with the behaviors you're now abandoning.
Do what you can to put it right. Every so often, come back to how you got to be someone who could do that, until you understand the pattern well enough that it can't drive you anymore.

This power to remove people is so easily abused, though. So work out the process before it’s about anyone in particular. What counts as cause for immediate protective action? Who has to step aside because they’re too close to it, and who decides to put temporary restrictions on someone? Who will make sure all the evidence is preserved? How will the person be able to reply to the concerns, and what review or appeal is possible without endangering others? What protections will there be for the person’s interests (housing, records, family contact, access to common resources, outside funds if any) during the separation? And when is it time to bring in outside help?

To turn this off, stop rehearsing it, take it out of any recordings you have and any apps that are active, and go back to the regular induction you’ve been using. Say that you won’t use it anymore when you’re awake, but realize that just saying it’s gone won’t make it go away immediately. If you find you’re responding to it when you don’t want to, or you’re having trouble with disorientation after using it, get some help from someone qualified. You can keep it in if you want, but only for starting a session later, when you want to. For now, today’s trance will be over when you come out of it.
When you do come out, reverse anything you’ve done to alter your state. If you’ve floated, regain your weight (of your choice, of course). Shrunk? Grow back to your normal size. If you’ve regressed or met parts, come back to feeling complete in the here and now, and acknowledge that your body belongs to you and is under control of the adult mind. And if you’ve gone somewhere, come back the same way you went. Etcetera. Make sure the only things you bring out with you are the ones you want to.

The closest thing I can compare it to is the out-of-body part of some near-death experiences. People sometimes report seeing things from impossible angles, and some of those reports (controversially) were verified by others in the room. My room event had nothing like that to check, though (I wasn’t floating around noticing any details), so those cases can’t back mine up. They just help me show what I mean by an experience that wasn’t stuck at the body’s vantage point anymore. If you want to go down that rabbit hole, there’s this systematic analysis of near-death reports, the AWARE-II cardiac-arrest study, and a recent veridical-NDE evidence scale.

After the day, look at what actually happened. If you did the Protector action(s) and didn’t feel better right away, that’s information to learn from, and it doesn’t mean you failed. Healing doesn’t go in a straight line, and standing up for yourself can make you feel worse at first. Not doing it is harder to figure out. Fear is the first guess, but maybe you didn’t know how or why. Being worn out can stop you too, and sometimes whoever said they’d help couldn’t make it. Hey, we’ve all been there. 🤗

Once you’ve got your bearings, make your first wish.
"Please show me the next truth. The next symbol or feeling. The question or action that's useful for me at this time, and no more than I can handle."
Stay awake when your mind likes to escape
If your mind keeps drifting off, sit up and open your eyes. Then feel your feet on the floor, and just let your breathing go at its own pace. Tell yourself, "I'm not going anywhere. I'm happily arriving more fully here each moment."
Pick something in the room to look at, and feel your spine at the same time (focusing on two things makes it harder for the mind to use multitasking mode to wander). Then ask yourself what the daydreaming is doing for you. Is it bringing you guidance? Maybe it's helping you work through a feeling. Or are you using it to avoid something?
Ask for any diffuse benefits to become more practically focused: "If this is guidance, show me what I need to do about it. If I'm avoiding something, bring me gently back to the present and show me what it is."
Make the hypnosis more alert
Aside from focusing on things in your direct experience, you can also suggest yourself into greater alertness (it's still relaxed-alert, not paranoid-alert). Keep your eyes open. Use a small hand movement each time you make the auto-suggestion that you're gaining increasing clarity. Then stop the hand movement and see where your mind is at. That hand movement is the mental escape into the body's flow. Say something like,
“Starting with your eyes open, press your thumb to your forefinger, gently, and let go. As you do, you begin to bring yourself into a place of clearer awareness… Press and let go again, and you’re clearer still. And once more, into the clearest state of awareness yet. Now stop pressing. In the first second after you stop, notice if there’s any echo of the pressing in your fingers, in your breathing, in your attention, or nowhere at all. Just notice, sit up straight and work from this level.”

How Much Happiness Do You Know Is Possible?
What do you picture when you wish someone well? Probably them fed and safe, with people around who like them, stuff like that. Wanting that for somebody is love (babies get this part already), and practical love matters a lot. How far my wishes for someone can go depends partly on how much happiness and peace I know are possible, and how much freedom.
But maybe you’ve had a big spiritual experience, and for a while you felt a peace or a love you didn’t know existed. After that, “I want you to be happy” can mean something much bigger, almost overnight. That’s why loving-kindness meditation can sound comically simple to someone who’s never been near that, and so powerful to someone who has. Saying “may you be happy” over and over won’t zap you into profound love, but it’s one way people find that love and grow it.
If that bigger happiness makes you curious, I’d follow the curiosity and skip pretending to believe anything. Read people from a few different traditions, say a Sufi poet and a Zen teacher. And if you ever meet someone who’s happy in a way that doesn’t add up, watch how they treat people on a day when everything’s going wrong for them.
Sometimes your little one has enough care, and what’s missing is something else. A hot meal can help, and so can saying no to your boss, but is that actually targeting the deeper existential question underneath? Life shouldn’t be just something you endure, like a hamster wheel or a rat race. What would you need to bring zest to a life of discovery?
Curiosity can be enough here, something like “Other people say they’ve felt a depth of love or peace that I never have. I don’t know if I believe their explanation. But what if the experience is possible for me?”

Sometimes a session goes great, and a few days later you’re skipping lunch and saying yes to everything again. I don’t think going deeper next time would fix that. I’d guess you just haven’t brought any of it out with you yet. Whatever you did for your little one in there, try a tiny bit of it out here, like texting a friend that you’re having a rough day instead of saying you’re fine.

After the day, look at what actually happened. Say you did the Protector action(s) and you don’t feel any better, or you feel worse. Standing up for yourself can do that at first. If you didn’t do it, that’s harder to figure out. Fear is the first guess, but maybe you didn’t know how or why. Being worn out can stop you too, and maybe whoever said they’d help couldn’t make it. 🤗

Sometimes the session itself goes really well. You feel real care for your little one and say exactly what they needed to hear, and then a few days later you’re skipping lunch and saying yes to everything again. A lot of people’s first guess is that they didn’t go deep enough. I don’t think that’s it, though, and I don’t think this one failed either. Maybe the grown-up just hasn’t come out of the exercise with you yet. Whatever you did for your little one in there, I’d try a tiny bit of it out here, because one small thing like that can teach them more than ten more good meditations. Texting a friend that you’re having a rough day instead of saying you’re fine is one, and that can be harder than the meditation was.

If nothing comes, that’s fine for now. You set this up as a healing session, but that’s no reason to answer for that part. Even without the answer, you can notice what sets the reaction off, and understand what it’s pushing you toward, and away from.

Say you keep getting confused or spaced out afterward, again and again. Those milder reactions count as caution signs too. Get professional help right away if any of this is severe or risky, and especially if it keeps going or comes back while you’re sober. If you think a prescribed medicine, or anything your body is dependent on, might be part of the problem, don’t quit it suddenly. Have a doctor help you stop safely.

I think most people who chase spiritual freedom are also trying to get away from something painful in themselves, and a lot of it goes back to childhood. That’s called spiritual bypassing. Plenty of seekers and gurus do it (I’ve written about the Dalai Lama as one example), and so did I. It doesn’t mean you’re stupid or crazy.

Inner child love
Put your hand over your heart and your other hand on your solar plexus (the two-hand practice in Working with your inner child), and say to yourself in a loving way, “Little one, you are not alone. You don’t have to fix this problem. I’m here now to listen to you.” Make sure you're actually talking to your inner child, not just repeating a script. If there’s no warmth today, rest your hands there anyway and notice what you find, no faking required.
Anxiety script
A script you could use for anxiety is:
Where are my body parts? What are my feet doing? How is my body positioned in the chair? How is my body breathing? How is my body situated in the room?
If you’re there, little one, I’m here. Thank you, guard, for letting me know you’re here. You didn’t have to scream. I got your message.
If there is something we need to do, let me know what the first thing is that we need to do at this moment. If there is nothing to do, help my body stand down. I’m not going to abandon you, but I’m not going to worship you either. I will listen to what you have to say and reality test it and then take some action.

And the parts just keep coming: managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts... At some point it’s a maze, with a little one somewhere in the middle of it. Some practitioners are gentle about it and walk you through the maze just fine. Others seem to leave people more split up than when they started. You can’t tell from a big institute and a pile of certificates whether a model is true, or whether it’s safe for you.

Say you keep coming back from trip after trip confused or spaced out. That’s the milder stuff, but it counts too. If it gets bad, or it keeps happening when you’re sober, don’t put off seeing a psychiatrist about it. And if you think a medicine you’re on is part of the problem, ask your doctor before you stop. Some, like benzos, can be dangerous to quit all at once, and so can alcohol once your body depends on it.

As for telling whether it helped, a few hours of feeling lighter, with the old feeling back the same day, is a few hours of relief. I’d take that! I just wouldn’t call the problem solved from it, or give the exercise all the credit, especially if you also slept well for once. Jot down what changed and how long it lasted if you want, and then leave it alone.
How many tries is enough? I really don’t know, and I’d be suspicious of anyone who promises you a number, including you, since some things shift in a day and some take about as long as learning guitar. If it’s making things worse, or you just can’t do it right now, I’d change course sooner (stopping counts). Not wanting to do it anymore is a reason too, but if that “nope” sounds like a part of you that’s trying to protect you, I’d hear it out first. If it still says no, that’s your answer. And if you keep doing the reparenting steps correctly and still don’t get the results you’d expect, ask yourself whether you have a unique case these steps don’t match yet. Maybe you’ll find something that works better for you, or you can ask me what I’d do for this case, or ask a therapist you work with. Either way, I’d like to hear about it!
